Here I redefined the target variable by classifiying any moments with readmitted == <30 as 30-day readmissions, and the other encounters as not redmitted within 30 days.

< 30 days = 11,357

Only 11% of the encounters are readmitted within 30 days. This is important because the model can predict “No” for almost everyone and it would still look accurate.

#replaces any  missing values with "?"
diabetes = diabetes.raw %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~na_if(.x, "?"))) %>% 
  mutate(
    readmit30 = if_else(readmitted == "<30", 1, 0),
    readmit30 = factor(readmit30, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

#check for missing values
diabetes %>% 
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "missing_count"
               ) %>% 
  arrange(desc(missing_count))
diabetes.clean = diabetes.raw %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~na_if(.x, "?"))) %>% 
  mutate(
    readmit30 = if_else(readmitted == "<30", "Yes", "No"),
    readmit30 = factor(readmit30, levels = c("Yes", "No"))
  ) %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    -weight,
    -encounter_id, #identifier var
    -patient_nbr, #identifier var
    -readmitted
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), ~replace_na(.x, "Uknown")),
    across(where(is.character), as.factor)
           
  )

Decided not to impute the missing values because there is a large count of variables that are missing information. Imputing the variable can add noise/fake certainty. Therefore, missing values were coded as ? were converted to NA. Weight was dropped because it was missing for most of its encounters 98569/101766 which could become less interpretable. Category variables with low/moderaye missing values were kept as “unknown” so that the model can capture the potential information.

diabetes.clean %>%

#checking fpr unique categories 
diabetes.clean %>% 
  summarise(across(where(is.factor), n_distinct)) %>%

The number of unique categories each variable has was checked. Diagnosis variables like diag_1, diag_2, and diag_3 had many unqiue diagnosis level so we need to group them into a broader category before modeling to improve interpretability.

diagnosis_grouping = function(x){
  x = as.character(x)
  x_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  
  case_when(
    x == "Unknown" ~ "Unknown",
    str_detect(x, "^[VE]") ~ "External/Supplemnetary",
    x_num >= 250 & x_num < 251 ~ "Diabetes",
    x_num >= 390 & x_num <= 459 ~"Circulatory",
    x_num >= 460 & x_num <= 519 ~"Respiratory",
    x_num >= 520 & x_num <= 579 ~"Digestive",
    x_num >= 580 & x_num <= 629 ~"Geniturinary",
    x_num >= 710 & x_num <= 739 ~"Musculoskeletal",
    x_num >= 800 & x_num <= 999 ~"Injury",
    TRUE~ "Other"
  )
}

#applying to the 3 diagnosis vars
diabetes_model = diabetes.clean %>% 
  mutate(
    diagnosis1_group = diagnosis_grouping(diag_1),
    diagnosis2_group = diagnosis_grouping(diag_2),
    diagnosis3_group = diagnosis_grouping(diag_3),
    across(ends_with("_group"), as.factor)
  ) %>% 
  dplyr::select(-diag_1, -diag_2, -diag_3) %>% 
  mutate(
    readmit30 = factor(readmit30, levels = c("Yes", "No")) #ensuring that readmit is a factor
  )

  
#checking the factor levels
diabetes_model %>% 
  summarise(across(where(is.factor), n_distinct)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "n_levels"
  ) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n_levels))
#removing the variables with only 1 level
diabetes_model = diabetes_model %>% 
  dplyr::select(-examide, -citoglipton)

Before grouping diagnosis variable had over 700 level now each group has only 9 level which is much easier to use and explain in a model. Also removed examide and citoglipton because each variable had 1 category and the model cannot learn nor change with just 1 level.

Model development

library(tidymodels)
## ── Attaching packages ────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels 1.3.0 ──
## ✔ broom        1.0.7     ✔ rsample      1.2.1
## ✔ dials        1.4.0     ✔ tune         1.3.0
## ✔ infer        1.0.7     ✔ workflows    1.2.0
## ✔ modeldata    1.4.0     ✔ workflowsets 1.1.0
## ✔ parsnip      1.3.1     ✔ yardstick    1.3.2
## ✔ recipes      1.1.1
## ── Conflicts ───────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels_conflicts() ──
## ✖ scales::discard() masks purrr::discard()
## ✖ dplyr::filter()   masks stats::filter()
## ✖ recipes::fixed()  masks stringr::fixed()
## ✖ dplyr::lag()      masks stats::lag()
## ✖ yardstick::spec() masks readr::spec()
## ✖ recipes::step()   masks stats::step()
diabetes_split = initial_split(
  diabetes_model,
  prop = 0.80,
  strata = readmit30
)

diabetes_train = training(diabetes_split)
diabetes_test = testing(diabetes_split)
diabetes_recipe = recipe(readmit30 ~ ., data = diabetes_train) %>% 
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) %>%  #removes vars with no variation
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.01) %>% #groups levels that are rare in other
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%#converts categorical vars into dummy vars
  step_zv(all_predictors())
logReg_model = logistic_reg() %>% 
  set_engine("glm") %>% 
  set_mode("classification")

logReg_wf = workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(diabetes_recipe) %>% 
  add_model(logReg_model)

logReg_fit = logReg_wf %>% 
  fit(data = diabetes_train)
logReg_predictions = predict(logReg_fit, diabetes_test, type = "prob") %>% 
  bind_cols(predict(logReg_fit, diabetes_test, type = "class")) %>% 
  bind_cols(diabetes_test %>% 
              dplyr::select(readmit30))
#accuracy & kap
logReg_predictions %>% 
  metrics(truth = readmit30,
         estimate = .pred_class)
#ROC
logReg_predictions %>% 
  roc_auc(truth = readmit30, .pred_Yes)
#PR_AUC
logReg_predictions %>% 
  pr_auc(truth = readmit30, .pred_Yes)
#CM
logReg_predictions %>% 
  conf_mat(truth = readmit30, estimate = .pred_class)
##           Truth
## Prediction   Yes    No
##        Yes    36    45
##        No   2236 18037

Accuracy = 0.888 ROC-AUC = 0.636 PR-AUC = 0.188

From CM: out of all true 30 day readmission: 32+ 2240 = 2272 model only correctly found = 32

recall is 32/2272 = 0.014–> model identifies about 1.4% of actual 30 day readmission with a 0.5 threshold

The baseline logistic regression model achieved a high accuracy but this is not correct because the outcome variable was highly imbalanced. The model predicted almost all patients as not readmitted within 30 days. The ROC-AUC was 0.636, CM showed that only 32/2272 true 30-day readmission were correctly identified at the default threshold. The problem is with the threshold because the foal is identify patients who may need post discharge care services. So we need to change the threshold and priotize recall, precision, PR-AUC, and cost based net financial value

tuning threshold to find an optimal option

tuning.threshold = tibble(
  threshold = seq(0.05, 0.50, by = 0.05)
) %>% 
  mutate(
    metrics = map(threshold, ~ {
      logReg_predictions %>% 
        mutate(
          prediction_threshold = factor(
            if_else(.pred_Yes >= .x, "Yes", "No"),
            levels = c("Yes", "No")
          ) 
            
        ) %>% 
        summarise(
          true_positives = sum(prediction_threshold == "Yes" & readmit30 == "Yes"),
          false_positives = sum(prediction_threshold == "Yes" & readmit30 == "No"),
          false_negatives = sum(prediction_threshold == "No" & readmit30 == "Yes"),
          true_negatives = sum(prediction_threshold == "No" & readmit30 == "No"),
          recall = true_positives / (true_positives + false_negatives),
          precision = true_positives / (true_positives + false_positives),
          flagged_patients = true_positives + false_positives
        )
    })
  ) %>% 
  unnest(metrics)

tuning.threshold

A threshold of 0.50 is not appropriate for this readmission problem. Lower threshold improved recall but increased the number of patients flagged for intervention –> creates a tradeoff between identifying more high risk patients and managing limited resources. The final threshold should be selected using the model performance and the cost/value assumptions.

cost and value analysis

#values are under assumptions
cost_per_readmisson = 12000 #readmission cost is $12000
cost_per_intervetion = 200 #post dischae intervention cost is $200/patient
intervention_effectiveness = 0.20 #intervention prevents 20% of readmission among flagged patients

#calculating the net financial 
cost.value.Results = tuning.threshold %>% 
  mutate(
    expected.readmission.avoided = true_positives * intervention_effectiveness,
    estimated.savings = expected.readmission.avoided * cost_per_readmisson,
    intervention.cost = flagged_patients * cost_per_intervetion,
    net.financial.value = estimated.savings - intervention.cost
  ) %>% 
  arrange(desc(net.financial.value))

cost.value.Results
#identifying the best threshold
cost.value.Results %>% 
  slice_max(net.financial.value)

The cost/value results showed that a 0.10 risk threshold produced the highest net financial value under the initial assumptions. With a threshold of 9,393 patients were flagged for enhanced post-discharge support, 1429 true 30-day readmission were identified, and the model achieved a recall of 62.9%. Assuming the cost od $12,000 per readmissionm an intervention cost of $200 per patient and 20% intervention effectiveness, this threshold proced an estimated net financial value of $1,551,000. This suggest that the threshold selection should be based on model performance, intervention cost, expected savings, and available care managament capacity.

cost.value.Results %>% 
  dplyr::select(threshold, recall, precision) %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(recall, precision),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x= threshold, y = value, linetype = metric))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+

The plot shows there is a tradeoff between having more readmission and avoiding unnecessary interventions

Chart interpretation: The threshold visualizations show that model performance has to be interpreted as a business tradeoff. Lower risk threshold identify more patients and improve recall, but it also increases the number of patients requiring intervention. At a higher threshold shows reduced care management workload and improve precision, but it misses more true 30-day redamissions. The net financial value chart combines these tradeoffs by estimating the expected savings from avoided readmission minus the cost of interventions. Therefore, a 0.10 threshold produced the highest estimated net financial valye, but the preferred threshold may change if intervention costs, staffing capacity, readmission cost, or intervention effectiveness change.

Model Comparision

library(ranger)
#defining the model
rf.model = rand_forest(
  trees = 100, #model building 500 decision trees 
  mtry = 10,
  min_n = 20
) %>% 
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>% 
  set_mode("classification")
rf.wf = workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(diabetes_recipe) %>% 
  add_model(rf.model)
set.seed(123)

rf.fit = rf.wf %>% 
  fit(data = diabetes_train)
rf.predictions = predict(rf.fit, diabetes_test, type = "prob") %>% 
  bind_cols(predict(rf.fit, diabetes_test, type = "class")) %>% 
  bind_cols(diabetes_test %>% select(readmit30))
rf.predictions %>%
  metrics(truth = readmit30, estimate = .pred_class)
rf.predictions %>%
  roc_auc(truth = readmit30, .pred_Yes)
rf.predictions %>%
  pr_auc(truth = readmit30, .pred_Yes)
rf.predictions %>%
  conf_mat(truth = readmit30, estimate = .pred_class)
##           Truth
## Prediction   Yes    No
##        Yes    14     5
##        No   2258 18077

The RF model had a slightly higher ROC-AUC and PR-AUC than the LR model. Though, at the 0.50 classification threshold it still identified very few true 30-day readmission. Therefore, will need to tune the threshold for the model.

Tuning threshold for RF

rf.threshold = tibble(
  threshold = seq(0.05, 0.50, by = 0.05)
) %>% 
  mutate(
    metrics = map(threshold, ~ {
      rf.predictions %>% 
        mutate(
          prediction.threshold = factor(
            if_else(.pred_Yes >= .x, "Yes", "No"),
            levels = c("Yes", "No")
          )
        ) %>% 
        summarise(
          true_positives = sum(prediction.threshold == "Yes" & readmit30 == "Yes"),
          false_positives = sum(prediction.threshold == "Yes" & readmit30 == "No"),
          false_negatives = sum(prediction.threshold == "No" & readmit30 == "Yes"),
          true_negatives = sum(prediction.threshold == "No" & readmit30 == "No"),
          recall = true_positives / (true_positives + false_negatives),
          precision = true_positives / (true_positives + false_positives),
          flagged_patients = true_positives + false_positives
        )
    }) 

  ) %>% 
unnest(metrics)
rf.threshold

For the RF model, a threshold of 0.15 would be practical as it flagged 5,126 patients, identified 952 true 30-day readmission, achieved a 41.9% recall, and provided a more realistic balance between readmission detection and resource constraints.

–> the threshold will be adjusted in accordance to the staffing capacity, intervention cost, and expected financial value.

cost/value ananlysis for RF model

rf.cost.value = rf.threshold %>% 
  mutate(
    expected.readmission.avoided = true_positives * intervention_effectiveness,
    estimated.savings = expected.readmission.avoided * cost_per_readmisson,
    intervention.cost = flagged_patients * cost_per_intervetion,
    net.financial.value = estimated.savings - intervention.cost
  ) %>% 
  arrange(desc(net.financial.value))

rf.cost.value

The RF cost/value analysis showed that at a 0.10 threshold it produced the highest estimated net financial value under the initial assumption. The model flagged 11,159 patients, identified 1,636 true 30-day readmissions, achieved 72.0% recall, and produced an estimated net financial value of around $1.69 million.

0.10 threshold = use based on max net financial value 0.15 threshold = use based on more capacity aware threshold

Model comparision and Recommended Threshold to use

model.comparison = bind_rows(
  cost.value.Results %>%
    slice_max(net.financial.value, n = 1) %>%
    mutate(model = "Logistic Regression"),
  
  rf.cost.value %>%
    slice_max(net.financial.value, n = 1) %>%
    mutate(model = "Random Forest")
) %>%
  select(
    model,
    threshold,
    recall,
    precision,
    flagged_patients,
    true_positives,
    expected.readmission.avoided,
    estimated.savings,
    intervention.cost,
    net.financial.value
  )

model.comparison

From the model comparison it showed that logistic regression and random forest performed best at a 0.10 decision threshold under the initial cost assumptions. The RF model identified 1,636 true 30-day readmission compared with 1,481 for logistic regression. It also achieved higher recall of 72% compared to LR’s 65.1%, and generated a higher estimated net financial value of $1,694,600 compared to $1,605,000. Therefore, the RF model is selected as the preferred model for the decision-support product. However, the selected threshold should remain adjustable because of intervention capacity, costs, and effectiveness may vary across hospitals.

Model interpretation: Variable Importance

library(vip)
## 
## Attaching package: 'vip'
## The following object is masked from 'package:utils':
## 
##     vi
rf.engine = extract_fit_parsnip(rf.fit)$fit
vip(rf.engine, num_features = 15)

The RF variable importance showed that the most influentials predictors included lab procedures, number of medications, prior inpatient visits, discharge disposition, time in hospital, number of procedures, number of diagnoses, emergency visits, admission type, admission source, and outpatient visits. These predictors reflect clincial complexity, prior healthcare ultiziation, and discharge-related factors. This support the business use case because patients with greater medical complexity or prior utilization may require more intensive post-dischare care-managment support.

Final Model Recommendation

Use the random forest model with a 0.10 threshold when the goal is to maximize estimated net financial value, while allowing the dashboard user to adjust the threshold based on available care-management capacity.
